essence.one_sentence: In a block sandbox the pleasure is reversibility: a block costs one click to place and one click to take back, so a 32 by 32 frame holds a whole world.
essence.summary: Empty square grid, one-click place and remove, a small palette of kinds, a hover that shows the target, a clear that starts over; no goal, no score.

llm_brief.text:
On the table: the user's words, quoted: "a simple block-building sandbox game with a 32x32 block world". Collected specifics: Fitts's law (time to hit a target grows with distance and shrinks with size; a grid cell is the target); Hick's law (each extra block kind is one more swatch to scan); visibility of system status (a placed or removed block changes on the next frame); user control and freedom (a mistaken placement is one click to remove); WCAG 2.2 target size minimum (24 by 24 CSS px, or spacing that keeps a 24 px circle clear); a canvas grid where one constant sets cell pixels and the click mapping (16 px and 64 px examples); the Sandboxels controls (left click draws, right click erases, one reset key, a readout of the cell under the pointer); a palette spread of two to five kinds (one fetched game uses four fixed materials, one reading among others; active swatch marked); a cursor that stands out from the blocks (one fetched game uses a translucent cyan square with a white outline that pulses; other treatments are options). Deep cuts from the pool: Conway's Game of Life tutorial (one value per cell, the grid redrawn each frame); Sol LeWitt's modular wall drawings (one rule per cell, the look built from repetition); toy brick sets (the snap of a placed unit); Tiled's placement preview on hover; falling-sand games (the cell as the whole model).

Ways in: a flat grid of square cells you click; a toy box with a palette of two or three kinds on number keys; stacked columns on a 32 by 32 base with a height cap; a paint stroke that lays blocks along a drag; a tile editor with a ghost of the chosen block and a text readout of the cell. Extra controls are options, not requirements: a clear button with a saved snapshot to return to, or pause and reset keys (opt-minimal-tools).

Dials: cell size from about 10 to 24 px (a 320 to 768 px world); block kinds from one to eight, three to five for a small palette; undo from one step to a stack of 10 to 100; hover tint alpha 0.25 to 0.5, outline 1 to 2 px; a placement flash of 80 to 250 ms or none, with a fade on removal set against a pop on placement.

Worn paths: the usual move for sandbox is a score, timer or win check: fresher: a block count that reads progress, or a shelf of creative tools. The usual move for world is a bigger, scrolling or endless grid: fresher: the same 32 by 32 frame, all visible, with a drawn border at the edge. The usual move for block is a Lego-style brick with studs or a wall you collide with: fresher: a flat square cell the player places or removes. Falling or bouncing blocks: fresher: blocks that stay where placed. A title screen or popup over the grid: fresher: the grid drawn on the first frame, with the palette and a key hint in a corner. Survival or crafting layers: fresher: an open palette where a click changes a cell. A pre-built starter terrain: fresher: an empty world that the first click builds in. Filler words such as stunning or seamless: fresher: say what the cell does.

Open: the dimension (flat plane, columns with height, or voxels: three readings), the view (top-down), whether a body exists (a cursor, or a body that moves: both are readings), the number of kinds (two to five; a palette spread, no default count), and the delivery (a single HTML page with a canvas, a technical assumption).

ak-ex-goal-score.instead: Free building with no goal: the player sets the pace and reads the grid itself, with a live block count.
ak-ex-goal-score.text: Sandbox means free play with no goal, score or end state. A worn path adds a counter or a win check, which turns free building into a game with a target.

ak-ex-survival-layer.instead: The palette stays open at no cost, and a click changes a cell.
ak-ex-survival-layer.text: A worn path adds survival or crafting systems around the build. The words ask for building, so the palette and the grid carry the whole game.

ak-ex-prefilled-world.instead: The world opens empty, and the first block is the player's first click on a cell.
ak-ex-prefilled-world.text: A worn path fills the grid with terrain or a sample structure before the player acts. The job starts from an empty world the player builds in.

ak-ex-filler-adjectives.instead: Say what the cell does: its color, its hover outline, and what a click places or removes.
ak-ex-filler-adjectives.text: Empty intensifiers that add nothing to a build or a check.

ak-ex-front-screens.instead: The grid draws on the first frame, with the palette and a key hint in a corner clear of cells.
ak-ex-front-screens.text: A worn path opens on a title screen or covers the grid with a popup. The player came to see the empty 32 by 32 world at once.

ak-ex-bigger-world.instead: Exactly 32 by 32 cells, all visible at once, with a drawn grid and a hover outline on the target.
ak-ex-bigger-world.text: A worn path grows the play field past 32 by 32 or lets it scroll. A click past an edge places nothing, and the edge draws as a visible border.

ak-ex-falling-physics.instead: Blocks stay where placed; a physics reading is a different game, not a default.
ak-ex-falling-physics.text: Block-building is placing and removing cells on a grid. A worn path adds gravity or a physics body, so blocks drop, slide or bounce out of the plan the player made.

ak-block-obstacle.excluded_sense: an obstacle that stops movement, a wall to collide with, or a Lego-style brick model with studs
ak-block-obstacle.instead: a flat square unit cell of the 32 by 32 grid that the player places or removes

ak-sandbox-physics.excluded_sense: a physics sandbox, a test harness, or a game with goals and scoring
ak-sandbox-physics.instead: free building on a flat grid with no goal or score; a falling-sand physics sandbox is a separate reference

ak-world-level.excluded_sense: a whole level map or a scene graph
ak-world-level.instead: the 32 by 32 play field, a flat plane by default; a stacked or voxel world is an option

ak-simple-touch-hud.instead: a simple block-building sandbox game: a palette row, one clear control and the grid on the default page

ak-simple-tool-buttons.instead: a simple block-building sandbox game: a palette row, one clear control and the grid on the default page

c-place-play.text: Does one click on an empty cell put a block there, visible on the next frame?

test.spec: Play: click an empty cell near the middle with the first block kind selected. The cell shows that kind's colour on the next frame, and no other cell changes.

c-remove-play.text: Does a right-click take that block back out in one action, without a browser menu?

test.spec: Play: right-click the cell just placed. The cell is empty on the next frame, and no context menu opens.

c-clear-play.text: Does the clear key empty the whole world at once, and leave the grid ready for the next block?

test.spec: Play: place blocks in three cells, press C. Every cell is empty on the next frame. Click one empty cell: exactly that cell fills.

c-full-world-ending.text: What does the frame look like when every cell is full, then cleared, then used once more?

test.spec: Play: fill all 1,024 cells (drag across the grid or click each cell). Click 2 px past the right edge of the frame: nothing changes. Press C, then place one block. The full grid draws on every frame, the outside click changes nothing, and after the clear only the new block shows.

c-corner-cells.text: Do the corner cells and the far edge take a click, and does a click just outside the frame change nothing?

test.spec: Play: click cell (0,0), then cell (31,31), then cell (31,0). Each fills under the pointer. Click just past the right edge of the frame: no cell changes.

c-click-mapping.text: Does the hover outline sit on the cell under the pointer, and not one row above or to the side of it?

test.spec: Move the pointer slowly down one column and across one row, both at the default size and in a window scaled by CSS. The outline stays on the cell under the pointer.

c-target-size.text: How large is one cell at the smallest window a player uses, against the 24 CSS pixel minimum?

test.spec: Measure one cell in CSS pixels at 375 px wide and at a desktop width. Report the value. A cell under 24 px passes when a gap keeps a 24 px circle clear of its neighbour, as a 20 px cell with a 4 px gap does.

c-no-goal.text: Is there any score, timer, win state or end screen anywhere on the page?

test.spec: The page shows no score element, no timer, no win or end message and no level goal at any point of play.

c-first-frame.text: Does the first frame show the empty grid, with no title screen or popup covering it?

test.spec: Load the page. The first frame shows the 32 by 32 grid, empty, with the controls in a corner and no overlay.

c-simple-count.text: Do the controls stay simple for a block-building sandbox: can a player name each control on screen, and does each one place, remove, pick a kind or clear?

test.spec: List each control and text line visible at rest; mark any that does not place, remove, pick a kind or clear. Pass when the marked list is short and each entry earns its place.

c-physics.text: After blocks are placed and the player waits, do they stay where they were put?

test.spec: Place blocks in the top rows and wait five seconds. No block has moved or fallen.

c-hover-target.text: Does the target cell show what a click will change, before the click?

test.spec: Hover an empty cell, then a filled cell. The outline or tint is visible on the next frame and differs between the two.

c-keys-kind.text: Does a number key change the block kind that the next click places?

test.spec: Play: press 2, then click an empty cell. The cell takes kind 2's colour, and the palette marks kind 2 as active.

c-phone-width.text: At phone width, does the page scroll sideways, and does a tap land on the cell under the finger?

test.spec: Resize to 375 CSS px wide. No horizontal scroll. Tap a cell and check that the cell which changed is the one tapped. Report the cell size in CSS px.

prompt_clauses._about: The user's words, verbatim, from the prompt. Each clause is a requirement or a bound.

up-game.text: The thing made is a block-building sandbox game.

up-simple.text: The game is simple; the word bounds the build.

up-world.text: The world is a 32x32 block world.

craft_principles._about: Discipline rungs for a small block sandbox: principles from interaction design, accessibility and browser input, each tagged with its rung.

heading_path: Fitts's Law and Its Applications in UX

cp-fitts.text: Time to hit a target grows with its distance and shrinks with its size, so large, close targets are fastest to reach.
behaviors: A grid cell is the target: larger cells are faster to aim at than tiny ones
The place and remove controls sit where the pointer already is
Palette swatches near the screen edge are easier to hit
cp-fitts.principle: Movement time depends on how big a target is and how far away it sits.
signals: tiny cells on a laptop screen

cp-hick.text: Decision time rises with the number and complexity of choices, so every extra block kind slows the pick.
behaviors: Each added block kind is one more swatch to scan before a placement
The kinds used most can sit first and largest
A selected kind shown in one place needs no search
cp-hick.principle: Fewer options on screen at once make each choice faster.

heading_path: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design

cp-status.text: Nielsen's first heuristic: the game keeps the player informed through feedback, so each action visibly answers back.
behaviors: A placed or removed block changes on the next frame
The selected kind is marked on the palette
The hovered cell shows what a click will change
cp-status.principle: The player should always know what the last action did and what the next one will do.
signals: no visible change after a click

heading_path: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design

cp-exit.text: Players make mistakes, so removal and clearing should be cheap to undo or redo, with no long dialog in the way.
behaviors: A mistaken placement is one click to remove
Clear-all starts over in one action
cp-exit.principle: Reversible actions make trying things cost little, which invites building.
signals: no way back after a misclick

cp-pointer-cell.text: Convert the pointer to a cell index once: subtract the canvas box, divide by the cell size, floor, then clamp to 0 to 31.
behaviors: A CSS-scaled canvas shifts clicks unless the position is scaled by the box size, not the pixel buffer
Right-click needs contextmenu prevented or it opens the browser menu
A click on the far edge maps to cell 31 only after clamping
cp-pointer-cell.principle: Map in CSS pixels against the box that receives the pointer, then convert to cells once.
signals: clicks land on the row above

cp-wcag-target.text: WCAG 2.2 level AA: pointer targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or keep a 24 pixel circle clear of other targets, so undersized cells need spacing.
behaviors: A swatch under 24 CSS px needs clear space around it
Grid cells sized at or above 24 px meet the floor without extra spacing
Cells of 20 pixels with no gap fail, because each 24 pixel circle overlaps its neighbour
Cells of 20 pixels with a 4 pixel gap pass under the spacing rule
cp-wcag-target.principle: Size or spacing keeps a target from being hit by its neighbour; either one is enough.
signals: swatches or cells under 24 px with no gap
a 24 px minimum on buttons and menu rows

cp-sandbox-controls.text: A falling-sand sandbox binds drawing to the left click, erasing to the right click and picking to the middle click, names the hovered element in a readout, and gives reset a single key.
behaviors: Right-click erasing is the removal gesture players expect
The removal gesture is a second button on the same pointer, so removing costs no key press
A readout line names the cell under the pointer as it moves
One reset key clears the whole world
cp-sandbox-controls.principle: Keep place and remove on the pointer, give reset its own key, and show what is under the pointer in text as well as in the drawing.
signals: status line that changes on pointer move
right click handled without a menu

sb-input-mapping.text: The Boris example maps a click through the canvas box and a width scale; the Ivy example adds an offsetY term to clientY.
properties: scaled by canvas width over box width
behaviors: Subtracting the box and scaling by the width ratio keeps clicks aligned when CSS scales the canvas
Clicks use the same floor division as the draw, so a click on a drawn cell lands on that cell
sb-input-mapping.principle: Map the pointer through the element's own box, then divide by the cell size.
signals: Math.floor on pointer position minus box offset
a grid cell toggled on click

controls_and_view._about: Controls, view and feedback for placing and removing blocks. Readings side by side; no control scheme is the default. Researched facts (cv-preview-before-click, ctl-select-and-place, ctl-remove-and-undo, cv-escape-cancels, sb-minimal-tools, sr-cursor-outline, sr-touch-hud) sit beside the options that build on them.

options._about: options, not requirements: the touch pad, stats panel and extra tool buttons are scraped examples that pull against the simple bound on the default page; recovery after a clear is a choice the build makes.

opt-touch-hud.text: An option for touch players: a visible four-way pad and large Build, Dig, Swap and Clear buttons, with the stats in a dark top-left panel. It puts more on screen than the default page of a simple game needs.
behaviors: Stats stay visible while building
opt-touch-hud.principle: Touch needs on-screen targets for every key action; stats belong where the eye starts.

opt-minimal-tools.text: An option: a clear button and a saved snapshot to return to, with reset and pause keys from the Sandboxels controls page. Each one is a control beyond the palette row and the clear control.
behaviors: Save copies the current cell state and reset copies it back, which works as one undo to a chosen point
Clear empties every cell in one action
opt-minimal-tools.principle: A saved snapshot and a clear make repeated placing and removing safe without an undo stack.
signals: buttons for clear, save and reset beneath the grid
key hints in a controls list

opt-clear-recovery.text: Clear has no way back on its own, so a wrong clear wipes 1,024 cells. Choose how it is recovered, one option or a combination.

options.does: a second press or a short dialog before every cell empties
options.tradeoff: stops the one-press wipe; adds a step to a deliberate reset

options.does: restores the world as it was before the last clear
options.tradeoff: covers the common wrong clear with no extra prompt; a clear followed by more edits cannot be undone

options.does: keeps the last N actions, clear included, as small diffs
options.tradeoff: deeper recovery; more state to store

opt-clear-recovery.principle: A clear that empties the whole world needs a check before it runs or a way back after it; each option trades a prompt, a step or stored state.

cv-escape-cancels.text: Escape aborts a move, resize or rotate and reverts the objects to their starting state.
behaviors: A cancelled drag leaves the world as it was before the drag began
cv-escape-cancels.principle: A reversible cancel makes trying a placement cheap.

ctl-remove-and-undo.term: remove a tile with right-click, undo with Ctrl+Z
ctl-remove-and-undo.text: Hover over a placed tile and right-click to remove it; an accidental placement is undone from the Edit menu or with Ctrl+Z.
ctl-remove-and-undo.principle: Removal and undo are reversible, so a mis-click costs one step.

cv-place-remove.term: pointer actions that place and remove
cv-place-remove.text: Each scheme gives the same grid result with a different cost to a mis-click.

options.does: two buttons on one pointer
options.tradeoff: needs the context menu suppressed; no right button on touch

options.option: left places, Shift or Alt click removes
options.does: one button plus a modifier
options.tradeoff: modifier is easy to miss

options.option: click or drag paints, right drag erases
options.does: one stroke covers many cells
options.tradeoff: a stroke places cells not meant; needs undo

options.does: filled cell is removed, empty cell is placed
options.tradeoff: no mode, but one click has two results

behaviors: Removal on a second button costs no key press
cv-place-remove.principle: Make removal as cheap to reach as placement, and keep a mis-click to one step.

cv-target-shown.term: how the targeted cell is shown
cv-target-shown.text: The player should see which cell a click changes, and whether it places or removes.

options.does: one-cell stroke that follows the pointer
options.tradeoff: shows where, not what

options.does: translucent block on the empty cell
options.tradeoff: shows what and where; looks like an overwrite over a filled cell

options.does: one colour to place, another over a block to remove
options.tradeoff: tells the actions apart; needs a legend

options.does: status line names the cell (x, y) and its contents
options.tradeoff: precise; the eye leaves the grid

cv-target-shown.principle: Show the target cell and the difference between placing and removing before the click.

cv-keys.term: keys that select kinds and clear the world
cv-keys.text: Keys trade speed against collisions with browser shortcuts and the risk of one-press wipes.

options.option: digit keys 1 to N select kinds
options.does: one key per swatch, labelled on screen
options.tradeoff: fast for a few kinds; keys must match the swatch numbers

options.does: step through the palette in order
options.tradeoff: any count; slow to reach a far kind

options.does: empties every cell at once
options.tradeoff: one press can wipe a build; pair with undo or a confirm

behaviors: Ctrl or Cmd with Z, S, R or W is taken by the browser or system
A clear with no confirm and no undo loses the whole build
cv-keys.principle: Put the frequent action on the cheapest key and the destructive one behind a second step or an undo.

cv-touch-keyboard.text: At phone width the 32 by 32 grid is about 10 to 11 CSS px per cell, under the 24 px pointer target minimum.

options.does: one finger, two gestures
options.tradeoff: a 10 px cell misses without a larger target

options.does: second tap commits
options.tradeoff: two taps per block; no misplacement under the finger

options.does: grid larger than the screen
options.tradeoff: adds a view state and a pan gesture

cv-touch-keyboard.principle: Count the target size before choosing the touch path; the grid does not fit a phone at a usable cell size.

cv-redraw.text: A 32 by 32 canvas is 1,024 cells, so a full redraw per frame is cheap; what matters is that a hover change redraws.

options.does: rAF loop draws the whole grid
options.tradeoff: simplest; constant small cost

options.does: dirty flag set by place, remove, clear, hover move, palette change
options.tradeoff: zero idle cost; a missed flag means a stale view

behaviors: A hover outline that redraws only on click lags one cell behind the pointer
cv-redraw.principle: Every input path that changes what is shown must also trigger a draw.

cv-extras.text: Recovery is cheap at this grid size; the question is how much history the player can reach.

options.does: restores the last placement or removal
options.tradeoff: covers the common mis-click

options.does: keeps the last N actions as small diffs
options.tradeoff: deeper recovery

options.does: shows filled cells out of 1,024
options.tradeoff: progress number; one line of UI

cv-extras.principle: Ship the extras that make removal safe and show progress; each one adds state and UI.

cv-preview-before-click.text: Object creation tools show a preview of the object to be placed before any click, already on hover; tile and template tools are named as the most useful case.
properties: preview of object to be placed
behaviors: Hovering a creation tool shows what a click would place, before the click
The preview also makes the selected creation tool clear to the player
cv-preview-before-click.principle: The player sees what a click will place before committing to it, and the preview doubles as a cue for which tool is active.
signals: object shown under the pointer before a click

ctl-select-and-place.term: select a tile, then place it on the grid
ctl-select-and-place.text: Click a tile in the Texture box and it follows the cursor until a left click places it; placement is free by default, and the Tools menu's Grid Snap jumps it cell to cell.
behaviors: Selecting a tile arms placement: the next left click on the grid puts a tile down
Hovering a placed tile marks it for removal; the page describes no outline on the grid itself

cv-player-body.text: The prompt names no avatar; the cursor acts by default, and a body is one option to add.

options.does: pointer is the whole player; no movement, collision or camera
options.tradeoff: smallest rule set; the 32 by 32 world fits on screen

options.does: arrows move a highlight; Enter places, Delete removes
options.tradeoff: a keyboard-only path; second input model to keep in step

options.does: a character walks the grid and places in front of it
options.tradeoff: adds movement and collision rules the sandbox does not need

cv-player-body.principle: A body adds rules the grid may not need; it earns its place only where the grid cannot be reached without it.

cv-feedback.term: feedback after a placement or removal
cv-feedback.text: Showing the change on the next frame is the floor; anything more is a choice with a cost in clarity or noise.

options.does: cell appears or disappears on the next frame
options.tradeoff: clearest and cheapest; can feel flat

options.option: brief flash on the changed cell
options.does: cell brightens, then returns
options.tradeoff: shows which cell changed in fast strokes

options.does: short tone per change
options.tradeoff: confirms strokes by ear; needs a mute

behaviors: A fade on removal and a pop on placement tell the two apart without reading
A flash longer than the next click makes fast building look laggy
cv-feedback.principle: Make the change visible at once; the rest is a choice.

sr-cursor-outline.text: The target is a translucent square cursor with a bright white outline, and it pulses in opacity so the player can find it.
behaviors: Cursor marks the selected cell, and a pulse keeps it findable
sr-cursor-outline.principle: The cursor is the only aim aid, so it must stand out from the blocks.
signals: a pale outline on a cell

world_model._about: Options and readings for the 32x32 block world: how the cells are stored, what a cell holds, how edges behave, and the dimension. Options, not requirements; no reading is the default.

w-cell-store.text: A 32x32 world is 1,024 cells. The store can be a flat array indexed row times 32 plus column, a 32-by-32 nested array, or a map that holds only the filled cells.
behaviors: A flat array makes the click-to-index math one line (row * 32 + col) and needs a bounds check before it
A sparse map stores nothing for empty cells, so clear is a map reset, but every read needs a missing-key fallback
w-cell-store.principle: The store should make the click-to-cell and render-loop reads cheap and obvious; the count is small enough that size barely matters.

flat.fits_when: one loop over every cell is the main read

nested.fits_when: readability of the code matters most

sparse.fits_when: the world is mostly empty and clear is frequent

w-cell-value.text: A cell holds either nothing or one block kind. The kind can be a small integer index into a kind table, a string name, or an object with a kind and a state.
behaviors: An integer index keeps a 1,024-cell array small and makes the palette a lookup table
A kind-plus-state object lets a block carry extra data later, at the cost of more checks on every read
w-cell-value.principle: A cell that holds one value is the simplest model; extra per-cell state is a later addition, not a requirement of a simple sandbox.

value.option: 0 for empty, 1 to N for a kind
value.fits_when: the kinds are fixed and few

object.fits_when: blocks will carry state such as paint or damage

w-kinds.text: The kind count sets the palette: one kind, three to five kinds picked by number keys, or eight or more that need grouping. Each count changes the selection UI more than the grid.
behaviors: One kind makes the game a pure place-and-remove loop with no selection state
Three to five kinds fit a row of keys or swatches that a player can scan at a glance
Eight or more kinds push toward a grouped palette, which adds a second layer of choice
w-kinds.principle: Each extra kind adds one more choice to remember; the palette should stay small enough to scan in one look.
signals: one selected kind shown in the UI

tokens.kinds: 1 to 8, or 3 to 5 for a small palette

w-edges.text: Three readings for the edge: bounded (clicks outside 0 to 31 are ignored), wrapped (column 32 is column 0 and row 32 is row 0), or open (the world grows when a block is placed at an edge).
behaviors: Bounded keeps the 32 by 32 size a fixed fact the player can see from the frame
Wrapped removes the edge, so a block at column 31 neighbours column 0 and any neighbour rule must agree
Open changes the size of the world, which the fixed 32 by 32 frame does not allow
w-edges.principle: The word 32x32 suggests a fixed frame; bounded matches it directly, and wrapped or open are readings to name, not defaults.
signals: clicks outside the frame do nothing
never_implies: wrapped edges imply a neighbour rule, which the prompt does not ask for

w-dimension.text: Three readings of the 32x32 world, each a different click: a flat plane of one layer, columns with a height, or 3D voxels seen with depth.
behaviors: On a flat plane a click maps to one cell with a 2D offset and nothing else
On stacked columns the click must pick a height as well, usually the top face of the column under the pointer
On a 3D voxel view the click is a ray test, which adds camera and depth code
w-dimension.principle: The reading decides what a click means, so the view and the dimension must be chosen together.

plane.tradeoff: smallest code and the clearest click; the world has no depth

columns.tradeoff: a stacked feel; the click needs a face rule

voxel.tradeoff: depth cues and a view to orbit; the most code

w-decisions.text: The world leaves four decisions open. Each takes options; none is decided here.
w-decisions.principle: Choose the dimension first; the store, edge and kind count follow from it.
signals: the prompt says 32x32 block world, no height

sb-grid-cells.text: A block builder is a canvas cut into fixed-size cells, one stored value per cell, with grid lines drawn over the field.
properties: canvas sized to columns times cell size
behaviors: Canvas width equals columns times cell size, so drawing and grid stay in step
Each redraw fills the field and strokes the grid again
Cell-to-pixel and pixel-to-cell conversion use the same constant
sb-grid-cells.principle: One constant sets the coordinate system, so the drawn grid and the clickable grid cannot disagree.
signals: canvas width is a multiple of the cell size
a CELL_SIZE or cell_width constant at the top of the file

sr-grid-columns.term: column-stack grid and place or dig
sr-grid-columns.text: The grid is a set of columns; each press adds or digs one block in the selected column, and a column stops at height 8.
behaviors: Digging an empty column does nothing
Cursor clamps at the grid edge instead of leaving it
sr-grid-columns.principle: One press, one block, a hard cap: each action is small and easy to undo.

look_and_feel._about: Cell size, grid lines, block colours and outlines, hover marks and a legibility check for a 32 by 32 block grid. Values are spreads of several readings, illustrative unless a source says otherwise. Nothing here was measured by the build; no moodboard was built.

lk-grid-lines.text: The fetched canvas examples fill the field and then stroke a line at every cell edge on each redraw. The line tone is a choice: a light field with a mid-gray line, or a dark field with a dim line.
properties: 1 px line at every cell edge
line a step off the field tone
behaviors: Each redraw strokes the grid again, so the grid is drawn every frame rather than stored as an image
A line close to the field tone disappears at 10 px cells; at 20 px or more it still reads
lk-grid-lines.principle: The grid is what separates an empty cell from a block, so it must stay visible at the smallest cell size.
signals: grid stroked after the field fill

lk-cell-size.text: Thirty-two cells per side sets the world size; the screen caps the cell size. About 10 px fits a phone, 20 px a laptop, and 24 px meets the target floor but needs a pan.
properties: cell size from the smaller window side
fit to window or fixed size with pan
10 to 11 px per cell on a phone
behaviors: Fit to window shows all 32 columns at once, but a phone cell falls under the 24 px target floor
A fixed 24 px cell (768 px square) meets the floor and needs a pan or zoom on small screens
A 16 px cell (512 px square) is the middle reading: fine for a pointer, tight for a thumb
lk-cell-size.principle: One cell-size constant drives both the drawing and the click mapping, so the grid on screen and the clickable grid cannot drift apart.
signals: a CELL constant at the top of the file
canvas width equals 32 times the cell size

lk-block-outline.text: Three block treatments are open: a flat fill that covers the cell, a one-pixel darker edge, or a two-pixel inset. No fetched source compared them at this cell size.
properties: flat fill with two or three block colours
behaviors: A flat fill with no edge merges neighbouring blocks of one kind into one shape
A 2 px inset keeps the grid visible between blocks and leaves the whole cell as the click target
A bevel adds a highlight edge that reads as depth but competes with the grid line for the same few pixels
lk-block-outline.principle: A 16 px cell has room for one clear edge, so the edge does the separating and the bevel is dropped.
signals: blocks of one kind merge into a blob
a highlight line on the top and left

lk-hover.text: Three hover marks appear in the fetched pages: a pulsing translucent cursor, a preview before the click, and a readout of what is under the pointer.
behaviors: The pulse helps the eye find the cursor on a busy field
A ghost of the selected kind shows what a click will place before the click
Hovering a placed block marks it for removal in the tile editor, with right-click to remove
lk-hover.principle: The hover says what a click will do before the click does it.
signals: translucent square on the cell under the pointer

lk-legibility-check.text: A reader checks legibility on the running game with four measurable checks, not by eye alone.
properties: cell pixels at the smallest window
behaviors: Read the cell size at the smallest supported window; under 24 px the grid needs a pan or a note
Measure the grid line against the field; WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1 for graphics needed to tell parts apart (known rule, not fetched in this build)
Check each block kind against the field and its neighbour at the same 3:1
Check the hover outline against an empty cell and against a block
lk-legibility-check.principle: The grid is legible when each cell, kind and hover can be told apart at the smallest size the player uses.
signals: a pixel ruler on the cell
a contrast ratio written beside each colour pair

sr-palette.text: The palette is a spread of sizes and material sets, not one set to paste: two, three or five kinds, with the active one marked. One fetched game's four fixed materials is one reading among the others.

options.does: two number keys; lightness alone separates them
options.tradeoff: fast to scan; little range

options.does: three keys, one lightness each
options.tradeoff: scans in one look; no room for a fourth

options.does: five keys or Q and E to cycle
options.tradeoff: more to remember; needs hue too

options.does: one game's Sand, Wet, Stone, Shell
options.tradeoff: a finished set; one example only

sr-palette.principle: How many kinds and which materials is a choice the build makes; a selected state keeps choice cheap.

lk-block-colors.text: Kind colours are a spread, not one set: pick values far apart in lightness, then check that the two nearest kinds differ by lightness before hue.
behaviors: Two kinds, one dark and one pale, separate by lightness at 16 px
Three kinds spaced across the lightness range read as three tones
Five kinds need a hue spread as well as a lightness spread, or two will merge
lk-block-colors.principle: At small cell sizes a hue shift is only a few pixels, so lightness and a spread of hues carry the difference between kinds.
signals: two kinds that merge into one tone

sb-block-shape.text: Block shape is a choice among three: a flat square that fills its cell, a square outlined inside its cell, or a filled circle at one third of the cell, which one fetched example draws.

options.does: the block covers the whole cell, so neighbouring blocks of one kind merge
options.tradeoff: the clearest unit; needs an edge or grid line to separate kinds

options.does: a 2 px inset square, so a margin of the grid shows around each block
options.tradeoff: keeps the grid visible; the whole cell stays the click target

options.option: filled circle at one third of the cell
options.does: a dot centred in the cell with radius one third of the cell, at rounded coordinates
options.tradeoff: reads as a dot, not a block; the fetched example's choice

sb-block-shape.principle: The shape is a choice; each one trades how block-like the unit reads against how much of the grid shows through.

vocabulary._about: Brain-dump vocabulary for a 32x32 block-building sandbox: how people talk about it, quality readings, register keywords, influences. Seed material; it widens the task and does not define it.

q-simple.text: Simple bounds the build: the fewest parts that still let a player place and remove blocks.

readings.reading: one block kind and one click
readings.in_practice: A single block type; a click places it, a right-click or second click removes it; no menus at all.
Three to five block kinds in a row; number keys 1 to 5 choose one; the chosen kind is highlighted.
A small palette and one clear-the-world button with a confirm, nothing else on screen.

q-block-building.text: Placing and removing blocks is the whole core loop, so its feel matters more than any extra system.

readings.in_practice: A placement lands on the same frame as the click; removal is instant with a short flash.
Holding the button and moving lays blocks along the path, one per cell crossed.
The cell under the pointer shows a translucent block of the chosen kind before any click.

kw-technical.text: Engineering words for a grid world and its drawing.

kw-perceptual.text: How a block world reads at a glance.

kw-playful.text: Human words for a block builder and its play; the casual ones a player would type.

kw-cultural.text: Adjacent practices a model may not connect to a small block sandbox at first.

infl-lineage.text: Each lineage brings one quality to borrow; none is a style to copy.
contribution: Falling-sand games (Sandspiel, The Powder Toy): instant, reversible placement and a cell model that is only a grid
Conway's Game of Life: a cell grid where every cell is just on or off, so state stays tiny
Sol LeWitt's modular wall drawings: a square grid where each cell is one rule, so the look comes from repetition
Early city-grid builders: one tool on a grid, no goal, the pleasure of tidy placement
Toy brick sets: the snap of a placed unit, which the hover ghost can echo

q-sandbox.text: Sandbox means free play with no goal, so the screen can offer tools instead of a target.

readings.in_practice: No score, timer, win state or level; the world is just there to be changed.
Tools beyond blocks, such as a paint brush, an eraser and a fill, chosen from a shelf of icons.
The grid is written to local storage or exported as text, so a build survives a reload.
